title: Victoria is facing a $3b-a-year debt bomb
full_text:
Victorian government bond yields are at their highest levels since the global financial crisis after the 10-year rate hit 6 per cent, putting further pressure on a state budget already heaving under massive debt.
Australia's most indebted state faces a raft of fiscal challenges over the next five years, including the rollover of ultra-cheap COVID-era loans to much higher interest rates after the 10-year bond rate surpassed 6 per cent and a multibillion-dollar hole punched in the budget by the property market downturn.
The Treasury Corporation of Victoria said the bond rate increased by 30 basis points at the end of September after the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted the cash rate 25 basis points to 4.6 per cent. On October 2, the 2036 rate climbed to 6.01 per cent, according to Shaw and Partners.
During the pre-global financial crisis peak in mid-2008, the benchmark 10-year Victorian government bonds reached about 7 per cent.
Institute of Public Affairs chief economist Adam Creighton said the rising bond yields would leave Victorian taxpayers with an additional $3.1 billion annual interest bill once the $77 billion COVID-era debts begin to be refinanced at about 6 per cent between September 2031 and November 2037.
"[The 6 per cent rate] is the highest in this century, and it's a scary wake-up call for state governments because they have limited taxation capacity, and they have huge and rising costs," said Creighton.
"In the next five years, there's going to be a huge increase in interest costs even if they don't borrow a cent more, which isn't realistic."
An IPA report in August estimated NSW, Victoria, Queensland and South Australia collectively took out $226.5 billion of cheap long-term bonds during the pandemic with interest rates of less than 3 per cent.
While those bonds currently cost taxpayers just over $4 billion per year in interest, that figure would rise above $12 billion by the mid-2030s as the debt is refinanced at much higher rates.
That report was published six weeks ago based on a bond yield of 5.5 per cent.
Creighton said Victoria's COVID-era interest bill was likely to be $400 million higher than he had initially calculated based on the latest rate of 6 per cent. "There are going to be very hard decisions for Victorian governments. They either put up taxes in a state that is already the most taxed, or they're going to be cutting spending, which is politically painful but economically good," he said.
Victoria handed down its budget on May 5, before the federal government announced significant changes to property taxes that have placed downward pressure on house prices across the country.
The government forecast operating surpluses of $6 billion over the four-year forward estimates, and tipped cumulative cash deficits of $30 billion over that period. Net debt was projected to rise to $200 billion by mid-2030, while interest repayments were estimated to climb from $8.9 billion this financial year to $11.8 billion in four years.
With the budget in a cash deficit, Victoria will need to continue borrowing money to fund its services.
Economists say Victoria's budget position has likely worsened in the past six months. State Treasury officials will release a pre-election fiscal update next month, in the lead-up to the November 28 election.
Westpac senior economist Pat Bustamante last month said higher bond yields would add at least $800 million to Victoria's interest repayments over the next four years, while weaker housing activity would blow a $2.5 billion hole in revenue this financial year.
In a research paper published on Tuesday, UBS said the housing slump could leave state and territory budgets across the country $30 billion short in revenue over the forward estimates, while rising bond yields globally would lead to interest bills up to $12 billion higher over the next four years.
"Lower property tax revenue and higher interest expenses weaken government budgets. Governments may not fully offset these impacts with spending cuts or raising other sources of revenue," UBS said. "Deficits may widen, meaning that the fiscal tightening implied by budget forecasts in FY27, to 4 per cent of GDP from 4.5 per cent in FY26, might not occur."
A Victorian government spokesman said its borrowing was diversified across domestic and international investors and that all three credit rating agencies had reaffirmed the state's AA credit rating with a stable outlook.
"We are responsible, managing every dollar while being the only government on the east coast to deliver a surplus this year," he said.
"Revenue forecasts are routinely revised to reflect new information and the government is closely monitoring property market developments."
Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said she was committed to delivering a cash surplus by 2032. "We'll repair the budget through a hiring freeze on back-office bureaucrats, a cap on excessive public sector executive pay, and put an end to the government playing venture capitalist with taxpayer money."
"Only the Liberal and Nationals have a plan to repair the budget and deliver a government that works," she said.
